title: Explainable forests compare climate and extreme-weather malaria associations
summary: A random forest analyzed malaria incidence across 78 countries during 2000–2022, with later years and withheld countries reserved for testing. Temperature and rainfall contributed more strongly to model predictions than disaster-related population indicators. These country-level observational associations do not establish causal weather effects, individual infection risk or benefits from an operational early-warning system.

source_review.scope: Primary relevant Methods/results/limitations, exact primary front identity and current primary PubMed notice metadata; version dates distinguished.

evidence.tested: Country/year-held-out prediction, training-fold preprocessing and sensitivity analysis of ecological feature attributions.
evidence.unknown: Causality, individual-level effects and operational intervention benefit remain unestablished; surveillance estimates and omitted confounders affect ecological inference.
evidence.ai_role: Random forests learn nonlinear country-year relationships; SHAP compares the contributions of climatic and extreme-weather variables.
